label: Shared responsibility across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

mentor.diagnosis: You assigned a responsibility to the wrong party. The dividing line moves with the service model, and the exam picks the model deliberately.
mentor.rule: Your data, your accounts and your configuration are yours in every model, without exception. Everything else shifts to the provider as you move from IaaS toward SaaS.
mentor.tell: 'Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system' is IaaS only. A misconfigured storage bucket or an over-permissioned account is always the customer, whatever the model.
mentor.trap: SaaS feels like the provider handles everything, which is why public data exposure through a misconfigured SaaS permission is such a common real world breach. Configuration never transfers.

label: Containerisation vs virtualisation, and VM escape vs container escape

mentor.diagnosis: You treated a container as a lightweight virtual machine. They isolate at different layers, which changes the blast radius.
contrast: Only the application and its dependencies
Breaking the hypervisor to reach the host or other VMs
Breaking out to the shared host kernel
Weaker, because the kernel is shared
mentor.rule: Containers share the host kernel, virtual machines do not. That single fact explains the speed advantage and the weaker isolation.
mentor.tell: 'Strong isolation is required between untrusted tenants' favours virtual machines or dedicated hosts. Density and fast startup favour containers.
mentor.trap: Containers are described as isolated, and they are, at a weaker boundary. A kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host at once.

label: Air gap vs logical segmentation vs microsegmentation

mentor.diagnosis: You called a VLAN an air gap, or proposed an air gap where the system genuinely needs connectivity.
contrast: Physical: no network connection at all
Removable media, or someone quietly adding a link
VLANs and ACLs on shared hardware
Policy per workload, often software defined
mentor.rule: An air gap means no connection exists. If data still has to move, it is not an air gap, whatever the design document calls it.
mentor.tell: 'The system must never touch the corporate network under any circumstances' is an air gap. 'Must be reachable only by the SCADA management server' is segmentation.
mentor.trap: Air gaps degrade quietly in practice. The moment someone adds a management link or walks a USB drive across, the protection is gone, and the design still claims it.

label: IoT, ICS/SCADA, embedded and real-time systems, and why the usual advice fails

mentor.diagnosis: You applied an IT answer to an operational technology question. These systems invert the usual priorities, and the advice that is right for a server is often unavailable or actively harmful here.
contrast: Availability and safety first; an outage can be physical harm
Rare: vendor certification, no maintenance window, often no patch at all
Fifteen to thirty years, long past vendor support
May halt a process that cannot simply be restarted
Deterministic: an agent that adds latency breaks the function
mentor.rule: If the system runs a physical process, availability and safety outrank confidentiality, and the control that fits is almost always network isolation rather than anything installed on the device.
mentor.tell: A production line, a utility, a medical device, a building system, or any stem mentioning that downtime is unacceptable.
mentor.trap: Installing an endpoint agent on a real-time system is the answer that looks most diligent and is the one that breaks it. Determinism is a functional requirement, and extra latency is a fault.

label: The axes an architecture is traded on: cost, deployment, recovery, availability, scalability

mentor.diagnosis: You judged architectures as better or worse. The objectives list them as trade-offs, so the exam asks what you gave up, not which one wins.
contrast: Capital versus operating, and at what scale
Cloud is cheap to start and expensive at steady state
How fast can we stand it up
Fast to deploy often means less control over the substrate
How quickly can we restore after failure
Snapshot and redeploy is fast; stateful systems are not
What uptime does the design support
Redundancy and dispersion both cost money and complexity
Latency to the user or process
Centralising improves control and adds distance
Elastic designs add moving parts and new failure modes
Can some risk move to a provider
mentor.rule: Every architecture question is a trade. Name what the option improves and what it costs, and the answer is the one whose cost the stem has said is acceptable.
mentor.tell: A stem that states a constraint such as a tight budget, a short timeline, or an uptime requirement.
mentor.trap: Risk transference is the one people overread. Buying a managed service moves the work and some of the financial consequence. If the data is breached it is still your breach to report.

label: Centralised vs decentralised architecture, and what each concentrates

mentor.diagnosis: You assumed centralised means more secure because it means more control. It concentrates control and it concentrates consequence, which is the trade the exam is testing.
contrast: One place to set and enforce policy
Policy must be propagated and verified everywhere
Fragmented, with gaps between the pieces
Compromise or outage of the centre reaches everything
Contained to the part that failed
The centre is a single point of failure
Survives the loss of any one component
mentor.rule: Centralised buys consistency and visibility and pays in blast radius. Decentralised buys containment and pays in drift and blind spots.
mentor.tell: A stem asking what is gained or lost by consolidating management, or by letting regions run their own.
mentor.trap: Both are defensible and the exam's answer follows the stated requirement. A question emphasising consistent policy wants centralised; one emphasising survival of a regional outage wants decentralised.
